rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The episode shows what a believer, aided by God, can do when confronting a tyrant who claims divine power.
rows.anchor: Bakınız Allah’ın inâyetiyle bir mü’min bir tâgūta ne yapmış

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nemrud may have become arrogant at receiving sovereignty, or repaid its blessing perversely with disbelief.
rows.anchor: mağrur olarak -veya hükümdarlığının şükrânını ma‘kus bir surette küfran ile edâya kalkışarak-

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Nimrod imprisoned Abraham after he broke the idols, then later asked whom Abraham called people to worship.
rows.anchor: Rivayet olunduğuna göre Hazret-i İbrâhim putları kırdığı zaman Nemrud onu zindana atmış

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's proof is that God creates life and death, meaning that He originates both life and its opposite.
rows.anchor: hem hayat halk eder, hem memat demekti

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nimrod claimed the same power by executing one man and sparing another, evading Abraham's proof and making a threatened claim to lordship.
rows.anchor: iki adam getirtmiş, birini idam edip birini salıvermiş, “İşte gördün mü?” demiş

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham answers with a fitting rhetorical shift: God brings the sun from the east, so Nimrod should bring it from the west.
rows.anchor: İbrâhim “şu muhakkak ki Allah [878] güneşi meşrıktan doğduruyor, sen de mağribden doğdur bakayım!” dedi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disbeliever is left stunned and defeated; had he accepted truth instead of acting unjustly, he would not have fallen into darkness.
rows.anchor: kâfir tutuldu kaldı, mebhût ü mağlub oldu

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Creating life is a greater proof of power than changing the sun's course, but unjust people trivialize it and claim its power for themselves.
rows.anchor: Hayat halk etmenin hareket-i şemsi tebdil etmekten daha mühim

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arrogant people may be defeated by a forceful sign and still refuse faith; the same pattern applies to communities as well as individuals.
rows.anchor: Ferdler böyle olduğu gibi cemaatler de böyledir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A taghut includes an unbeliever who claims to rival God by saying that he gives life and death; a believer should plainly correct him.
rows.anchor: tâgūtun misâllerinden biri böyle “ben ihyâ ederim ve öldürürüm” diye Allah ile rekabete kalkışan kâfirdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's composure before Nimrod demonstrates God's favor: those without faith tremble before the tyrant, while Abraham overwhelms him.
rows.anchor: Allah’a imanı olmayanlar, bunun yanında korkusundan tiril tiril titrerken bak İbrâhim ona ne yapmış

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person can be king and remain unguided; sovereignty is a divine trust to govern by God's command and justice, not personal desire.
rows.anchor: kâfir, melik olabilir ve fakat bir kimse melik olmakla hidâyete ermiş olmaz

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Life and death are manifest truths, yet people who treat them as ordinary may accept life's origin while denying resurrection because they miss recurring examples.
rows.anchor: asl-ı hayâtı tasdik ederken ba‘s ü neşri inkâr ederler

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who place themselves above God's law and alter truth are destined to God's blow, dragging themselves and their subjects into ruin.
rows.anchor: teba‘alarıyla beraber kendilerini de zulümâta sürükler ve uçurumlardan yuvarlanır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Political sovereignty is a great divine blessing, but rulers possess it only as deputies rather than as its true owners.
rows.anchor: insanlar kendilerini bunun sâhib-i aslî ve hakīkīsi değil, sâhib-i niyâbî ve mecâzîsi bilmelidirler

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nimrod was deprived of guidance because he misunderstood delegated sovereignty, while Abraham prevailed through reliance on God.
rows.anchor: Nemrud bunu böyle tanımadığı için hidâyet-i ilâhiyeden mahrum zâlimlerden oldu

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The concise debate conveys divine support for believers and their proper conduct toward tyrants with clarity and eloquence; the verse is clear proof.
rows.anchor: bu âyet, ıtlâkıyla muhkemâttan olan bir âyet-i beyyinedir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's power to give life is not limited to one occurrence: He creates from nothing and can revive the dead in ordinary or extraordinary ways.
rows.anchor: Ma‘dûmu îcad edip hayat verdiği gibi meyyiti de tekrar ba‘s ile ihyâ edebilir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Life itself is miraculous, and God's bringing believers from darkness into light can exceed the limits of intellect and science without being impossible.
rows.anchor: Böyle olmakla beraber [880] bunlar akılların kabul edemeyeceği, reddine mecbur olacakları muhâlâttan değildirler

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some events seem inexplicable to unbelievers but become clear proofs to believers after they occur; God is about to give two such examples.
rows.anchor: Cenâb-ı Allah bunları da iki misâl ile[^12] beyan edecektir

rows.speaker: bazıları
rows.claim: Some grammarians treat the kaf in ka-alladhi as an extra particle for verbal elegance, since a prepositional kaf could not enter after the preceding construction.
rows.anchor: bu kâf’a مُقْحَم yani tahsîn-i lafz için gelmiş bir harf-i zâid diyenler olmuştur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other analyses take kaf as a noun meaning like, or connect the phrase by meaning as have you seen someone like this; the semantic link can yield or like this one.
rows.anchor: Fakat bunun مثل mânasına kâf-ı ismî olarak أَوْ اَلَمْ تَرَ إِلَى مثلِ الَّذِي demek olduğu ihtar edilmiş

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The explicit comparison directs attention to the event and exemplifies analogical and inductive reasoning from particular cases to general knowledge of God's power.
rows.anchor: meşhuddan gayr-i meşhûda intikal ile mümaselet kanunu mûcebince evvelâ kıyâs-ı temsîlî

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers should read the story alongside recurring life and death events rather than as an isolated wonder; every universal law began with one extraordinary event.
rows.anchor: münferid bir hârika olarak [881] değil, vücûh-ı muhtelifeden ibret-engîz vukū‘ât ile meşhun olan kıssasını bir misâl olarak alıp emsâliyle mülâhaza ediniz

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The village was a city whose roofs had collapsed, leaving buildings overturned and the place devastated and deserted.
rows.anchor: o sırada bu karye damlarının üzerine çökmüş, o mâmur binâların tavanları çöküp inmiş

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arsh primarily means roof, but can also designate roofed structures or anything that casts shade, allowing several visual descriptions of the ruin.
rows.anchor: “Arş”, esasen tavan demek olup müsakkafâta ve her tarafına gölge veren şeylere de ıtlak olunduğundan

rows.speaker: Hazret-i Ali, İbn Abbas, İkrime, Ebü’l-Âliye, Said b. Cübeyr, Katâde, Rebî‘, Dahhâk, Süddî, Mukātil, Süleyman b. Büreyde, Nâciye b. Ka‘b, Sâlim el-Havâs
rows.claim: These authorities identify the man who passed the ruined village as the prophet Uzayr.
rows.anchor: Hazret-i Ali, İbn Abbas, İkrime, Ebü’l-Âliye, Said b. Cübeyr, Katâde, Rebî‘, Dahhâk, Süddî, Mukātil, Süleyman b. Büreyde, Nâciye b. Ka‘b, Sâlim el-Havâs demişlerdir[^15] ki: “Bu şahıs Hazret-i Üzeyr idi”

rows.speaker: Vehb, Mücâhid, Abdullah b. Ubeyd b. Umeyr, Bekir b. Mudar
rows.claim: These authorities identify the man as Jeremiah, Ermiyâ.
rows.anchor: Vehb, Mücâhid, Abdullah b. Ubeyd b. Umeyr, Bekir b. Mudar, “Hazret-i Ermiyâ[^16] idi” demişler

rows.speaker: İbn İshak
rows.claim: Ibn Ishaq says that Ermiyâ was Khidr.
rows.anchor: İbn İshak da Ermiyâ’nın Hızır olduğunu söylemiştir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other identifications say the man was Lot's servant or Sha'ya; another view says he began as an unbeliever and believed after being revived.
rows.anchor: Bunlardan başka Lût aleyhisselâm’ın kölesi veya Şa‘yâ dahi denilmiş, bidâyeten bir şahs-ı kâfir ve fakat ba‘de’l-ihyâ mü’min olduğu da söylenmiştir

rows.speaker: Vehb, Katâde, Dahhâk, İkrime, Rebî‘
rows.claim: These authorities identify the village as Ilya, that is, Jerusalem.
rows.anchor: Vehb, Katâde, Dahhâk, İkrime, Rebî‘buna “İlyâ” yani “Beytü’l-Makdis” demişler

rows.speaker: Dahhâk
rows.claim: Dahhâk also reports a village two farsakhs from Jerusalem called Karyetü’l-Ineb, or identifies the site as the Holy Land.
rows.anchor: Dahhâk’tan Beyt-i Makdis’e iki fersah mesafede “Karyetü’l-‘Ineb” veya arz-ı mukaddes

rows.speaker: bazıları
rows.claim: Some identify the village as al-Mu'tafika.
rows.anchor: bazılarından Mü’tefike

rows.speaker: İbn Zeyd
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd identifies it with the city of the thousands who fled death, mentioned earlier in the commentary.
rows.anchor: İbn Zeyd’den bâlâda zikri geçen ve ölümden kaçan binler şehri

rows.speaker: İbn Abbas
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas places the village at the Monastery of Heraclius beside the Tigris.
rows.anchor: İbn Abbas’tan Dicle kenarında Deyr-i Hirakl

rows.speaker: Kelbî
rows.claim: Al-Kalbi identifies the village as Shaburabad.
rows.anchor: Kelbî’den Şâbûrâbâd

rows.speaker: Süddî
rows.claim: Al-Suddi identifies the village as Salmanabad.
rows.anchor: Süddî’den Selmâbâd diye de nakiller vardır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The best-known account identifies the man as Uzayr son of Sherehiya and the village as Jerusalem, destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar's campaign.
rows.anchor: en meşhuru şahsın Hazret-i Üzeyr b. [882] Şerhıyâ, karyenin de Benî İsrâil devletinin makarrı olan Kudüs şehri olmasıdır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account says Nebuchadnezzar devastated Jerusalem, killing some Israelites, settling some in Syria, and carrying others into captivity; Uzayr later escaped and saw the city ruined.
rows.anchor: Buhtunassar’ın harbiyle istîlâ ve tamamen tahrip edilmiş ve bütün Benî İsrâil üç kısma tefrik olunup

rows.speaker: İbn Abbas
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas transmits in detail that this account was the occasion of revelation.
rows.anchor: İbn Abbas’dan sebeb-i nüzûlün bu olduğu bi’t-tafsîl mervîdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Revival miracles are also narrated for the alternative identifications, and the story's general sense may encompass one or several such events.
rows.anchor: diğerleri hakkında da böyle[^20] birer[^21] imâte ve ihyâ hârikaları mervî ve kıssanın mefhûm-ı umûmîsi her birine veya hepsine muhtemil bulunduğu gibi

rows.speaker: müfessirler
rows.claim: Some commentators read the episode as movement from unbelief's darkness and despair into faith, success, and hope; the author prefers its more apparent contextual sense as a prophetic miracle arising from a believer's grief.
rows.anchor: bu vak‘ayı zulmet-i küfürden nûr-i imana, yeisten muvaffakiyet ve ümide bir intikal misâli gibi telakkī eden müfessirler olmuş ise de siyâk-ı âyet bunun meşhûru üzere bir hârika-i nübüvvet olmasında daha zâhirdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The episode concerns a believer's grief, wish for revival, and confession of limited understanding, not absolute despair that constitutes unbelief.
rows.anchor: mevzû‘-i kıssa kâfirâne bir ye’sin değil, mü’minâne bir hüzn ü kederin netâicini

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People not hardened in unbelief may still be brought from disbelief to faith and made witnesses to wonders; God's guardianship of believers includes them.
rows.anchor: küfrü tabiat edinmemiş olanlar hakkında küfürden imana ihrâc ve o imanı hârikalara mazhar etmek de

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse's meaning is not restricted to Uzayr or Ermiyâ: the indefinite village and mentally understood comparison allow the account to fit multiple events.
rows.anchor: mefhûm-ı âyet tahsis edilmeyerek[^24] kıssa müte‘addid vukū‘âta muntabık olabilmek için “karye” nekre olduğu gibi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question may ask how, where, or when God will revive the village, expressing a wish for revival alongside uncertainty about its means and timing.
rows.anchor: 1. Edecek ammâ acaba nerden edecek? Nasıl edecek, ne zaman edecek?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It may express a wish for swift revival and grief at being unable to find its path, fearing that God may act too late for the speaker to see.
rows.anchor: Ben buna serî‘bir hayat temenni ediyorum, fakat âcizim

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third possible sense concedes that God can revive it but suspects He will not.
rows.anchor: Yapabilir ammâ galiba yapmayacak

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fourth possible sense denies that the dead can return at all; this would be absolute despair and unbelief.
rows.anchor: Ölen dirilir mi? Giden geri gelir mi? Bunun ihyâsına

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if the speaker did not intend outright disbelief, the phrase could imply it and become a verbal slip; believers should not despair, though human weakness can diminish hope.
rows.anchor: Bunun için bu sözü söyleyen bu maksadla söylememiş olsa dahi bu îhâm dolayısıyla bir lisan kayması[^25], bir zelle yapmış olur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Absolute despair and absolute security are both unbelief: despair cuts off hope in God, while security is arrogant presumption and a kind of separation from Him.
rows.anchor: yeis küfür olduğu gibi, emn-i mutlak da küfürdür

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even prophets may experience grief and a thought resembling lost hope, but divine aid arrives immediately because they are under God's protection.
rows.anchor: yeis değil, fakat ye’se doğru bir zan ve tevehhüm ile inkisâr-ı ümîd ve bu suretle bir gam ve elem peygamberler hakkında bile mümkindir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In such moments believers should cling more firmly to faith, seek help through patience and prayer, avoid despairing panic, and trust God's power to revive after death.
rows.anchor: ‘urve-i imana daha ziyade sarılıp sabr u salât ile isti‘âne etmek

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse expresses sorrow that draws divine aid, yet its hint of despair is a lapse; God begins relief while the desired result unfolds only after a century as discipline.
rows.anchor: bunun az çok bir îhâm-ı yeisten dahi hâlî kalmamış olması bir zelle olacağından

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God subjected the man to a death lasting one hundred years; a report says he fell asleep and died in sleep while still young.
rows.anchor: Rivayete nazaran bir uykuya dalmış, o uykusunda ölekalmış idi ve henüz genç idi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God then restored him to life with his former intellect, understanding, and capacity to reason about divine knowledge.
rows.anchor: Evvelki gibi hay, âkil, fehimli, ma‘ârif-i ilâhiyede nazar u istidlâle müsta‘id bir rûh ile ba‘s ba‘de’l-mevte mazhar etti

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says that in year seventy a Persian ruler named Yushek reconquered the Holy Land, Nebuchadnezzar died, survivors returned, and Jerusalem was rebuilt over thirty years before Uzayr was revived there.
rows.anchor: Bazı rivayete göre bu yüz senenin yetmişinci senesi “Yuşek” nâmında bir Fars hükümdarı tarafından külliyetli bir askerle arz-ı mukaddes fethedilmiş

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Uzayr guessed that he had stayed a day or part of one from the lingering memory of waking and sleep, estimating cautiously rather than lying.
rows.anchor: evvelki hayâtın uyku hakkındaki [885] bakıyye-i hâtırâtından bi’l-istidlâl tahmînen ve yalandan ihtirâzen bi’l-ihtiyat böyle söyledi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every future moment retains a memory of the past; sleep and death leave an initial, general recollection that links a person to the earlier self.
rows.anchor: Gerek uyku gerek ölüm bile ilk intibahta insana icmâlen bir hâtıra bırakıp da gidiyor

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Without this continuity of memory, an awakened person would think existence had just begun and say he was newly born.
rows.anchor: “kalmadım yeni doğuyorum” derdi

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because life connects past, present, and future, even a hundred-year life seems like a day when it ends; such experiences visibly illustrate the afterlife and resurrection.
rows.anchor: hayatta geçen yüz senelik bir ömür bile nihâyetinde insana bir gün gibi gelir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God corrects the estimate and tells him to inspect his food and drink, which have not aged or spoiled but remain fresh.
rows.anchor: şimdi yiyeceğine ve içeceğine bak, Allah’ın kudretini seyret ki {لَمْ يَتَسَنَّهْ} hiçbiri yıllamamış

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The donkey too is shown as part of the sign of divine power.
rows.anchor: Merkebine de bak, onu da öyle bulacaksın

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He was revived as a sign for people, not because his lifespan had ended, so that he could witness and attest to many kinds of resurrection with certainty.
rows.anchor: ve seni ecelin geldiği için değil mahzâ bir ibret için seni nâsa bir âyet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to look at the bones may concern his own, the donkey's, both, or bones in general, and calls for sight and insight.
rows.anchor: o kemiklere, yani kendinin veya merkebinin kemiklerine veya her ikisine, yahut ‘ale’l-‘umûm [886] kemiklere de bak

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The usual reading means raising and joining the bones in place; Nafi, Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr, Abu Ja'far, and Ya'qub read nunshiruhā, meaning reviving them.
rows.anchor: Nâfi‘, İbn Kesîr, Ebû Amr, Ebû Ca‘fer, Ya‘kūb kıraatlerinde noktasız راء ile انشار’dan نُنْشِرُهَا okunduğuna göre

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bones emerge and reassemble while flesh forms, grows, and covers them, producing a living body.
rows.anchor: o[^33] etler nasıl tekevvün ediyor, neşv ü nemâ buluyor, o kemikleri sarıyor da bir cism-i zî-hayât teşekkül ediyor

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The body's changing parts and enduring personal identity display death and revival continually; neither the parts nor the whole alone remain fixed, but God's power sustains them.
rows.anchor: Demek ki bütün bunlarda sâbit olan ne o eczâ, ne o küldür, ancak kudretullahtır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Life is everything and everything subsists through God's power; ignoring this leaves people unable to understand resurrection even while witnessing its patterns in their own lives.
rows.anchor: hayat her şeydir ve her şey kudretullah ile kāimdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the truth became clear, the man affirmed that God has power over everything; Hamza and Kisai read the verb as an imperative, God commanding him to know this certainty.
rows.anchor: Hamza, Kisâî kıraatlerinde emir sîgasıyla أَعْلَمُ okunur ki bu şüphe üzerine Allah o şahsa bu emr-i yakīnîyi verdi demek olur

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sound reason and science should recognize ordinary causes while remembering God's absolute right as the sovereign sustainer; forgetting it narrows thought and leads to denying established miracles.
rows.anchor: esbâb-ı tâliye ve mebâdî-i âdiyenin izâfî olan hakkını vermek isterken saltanat-ı kâinâta hâkim kayyûm-ı kül olan Allah teâlâ’nın hakk-ı mutlakını unutmamak lâzım gelir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God can revive by His own will and can also grant servants life and light so they may pass them to others, producing light upon light.
rows.anchor: Hayat ve nûr bahşettiği kullarına o hayat ve o nûrdan diğerlerine ifâza edecek bir ihyâ ve tenvir kudreti de verebilir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham asks how God revives the dead, not whether He can; his earlier confession that God gives life and death shows his faith in God's power.
rows.anchor: “yâ Rabbi” dediği zaman, “Ey ihyâ ve imâteye kādir olan Rabbim” diyor

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham wonders whether the life-giving power he knows in God can also manifest through him, and asks to see the manner of revival.
rows.anchor: feyz-i hayat gibi feyz-i ihyâ da bende tecellî edebilir mi? Tâyin edemiyorum da düşünüyorum

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God asks whether Abraham has not believed simply because he does not know the detailed manner; faith requires accepting God's unlimited power without seeing every modality.
rows.anchor: İman için görmek mi lâzım ki göster diyorsun?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's limitless power has innumerable modes that cannot all be seen, though He may show Abraham some as a sign.
rows.anchor: Kudret-i mutlaka-i ilâhiyenin ta‘ayyünâtı ise nâmütenâhîdir, onlar tamamen görünmez ancak îmân-ı mutlakla bilinir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham affirms belief and seeks tranquility, moving from knowledge toward witnessed certainty and the lasting life of the heart.
rows.anchor: ve lâkin kalbim mutmain olmak için, o imanın verdiği şevk ile kalbime düşen heyecân-ı ümîdi teskin etmek

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His longing is to reach the station of intimate friendship with God and remain God's Friend forever.
rows.anchor: makām-ı hullete erip ilelebed Halîlullah olarak kalmaktan ibaret bulunduğunu izhar etti

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report identifies the four birds as a peacock, rooster, crow, and dove, or alternatively an eagle.
rows.anchor: rivayete göre lâm-ı ‘ahd olarak tâvus, horoz, karga, güvercin veya nesr

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb fasurhunna has a kasra reading from ṣ-y-r and a damma reading from ṣ-w-r; both can mean turning or inclining, while cutting into parts is another reported sense.
rows.anchor: Hamza kıraatinde “sad”ın kesriyle, mütebâkīsinde zammıyla okunur. Zammı صور’dan, kesri صير’dan gelir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author favors the sense of inclining or joining the birds to Abraham, since the following words already make the cutting interpretation clear.
rows.anchor: mâba‘dinden de anlaşılacağı[^39] cihetle burada imâle kâfîdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham must know and internalize the birds' particular forms and identities; this gathering of their true essences in his knowledge is presented as a condition for revival.
rows.anchor: sırr-ı hayâta mazhar olan hakīkat-i hâssalarıyla tanınıp ilm-i İbrâhim’e idhâl

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The birds' return to Abraham after being divided and placed on mountains displays how divine will joins knowledge and action in revival.
rows.anchor: sonra onları çağır, bi-iznillâh hükm-i irâde ve ihyâ zâhir olsun

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aziz means God overcomes all possibilities and is ruled by no cause; Hakim means He orders effects, causes, and outcomes with wisdom.
rows.anchor: Evvelâ cemî‘-i mümkinâta gālib ve hâkim ve hiçbir sebebe[^40] mahkum ve mağlub olmaz bir sâhib-i izzettir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's use of ordinary causes reflects wisdom and ordered relations, not inability to create extraordinary events directly.
rows.anchor: Böyle ef‘âlinin esbâb-ı âdiye ve kavânin-i muttarideye ibtinâsı her birini hâriku’l-‘âde tarîklerle îcâddan âciz olduğu için değil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God could create every effect as a separate miracle, but then created events would lack the ordered connections and relations He has wisely established.
rows.anchor: Müsebbibü’l-esbâb olan Allah sebeb-i evvel ve fâ‘il-i â‘lâ olduğu için hiçbir sebep halk etmeyip her fiilini re’sen bir hârika olarak yapmaya da kādirdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Divine might and wisdom do not conflict: God controls all causes, and created causes have no independent force when He does not will their effects.
rows.anchor: Esbâba teşebbüs edildiği zaman O dilemezse hiçbir şey olmaz

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God may revive the dead directly or through particular causes; His might and wisdom appear in either mode, with initial creation especially showing might and subsequent creation especially showing wisdom.
rows.anchor: emvâtı da dilerse kendinden başka hiçbir sebebe merbut olmayarak ihyâ eder ve dilerse hikmetiyle esbâb-ı mahsûsa tahtında ihyâ eder

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God gives human faith and choice a special causal role, allowing voluntary return and resurrection toward chosen eternal life alongside compulsory return and resurrection.
rows.anchor: kullarının iman ü ihtiyarlarına dahi bir sebebiyyet-i [891] mahsûsa bahşetmiş olması

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The general statement that God has power over everything is expanded by the specific names Aziz and Hakim; Uzayr illustrates compulsory resurrection, while Abraham illustrates both modes.
rows.anchor: Üzeyr[^44] makām-ı icmâlde hükm-i izzetle ba‘s-i cebrîye, İbrâhim makām-ı tafsîlde hükm-i izzet ve hikmetle

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commands cannot be an impossible challenge: the context praises Abraham and divine power, and the commentators and reports agree that Abraham actually witnessed revival and attained tranquility.
rows.anchor: emr-i ta‘cîzî olmalarına ise hiçbir vecih ve karîne bulunamayacağı gibi, âyetin siyâkı münâfîdir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commands are legal instructions that also entail creative realization; Abraham's complete return to God enabled him, by permission, to witness some modes of revival.
rows.anchor: Bizce doğrusu bu emirler emr-i teklîfî olmakla beraber emr-i tekvînîyi mutazammındır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two narratives contain more mysteries than commentary can exhaust, but teach that sufficient knowledge of life and connection to the highest source show resurrection to be a matter of divine will and the command Be.
rows.anchor: ba‘s ü ihyânın bir irade meselesine, bir “kün” emrine râci‘olacağı görülecektir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Human memory offers an analogy: one can mentally divide and scatter a known image, then summon it back into its former form unless God causes forgetting or another impediment.
rows.anchor: bir insan nefsinde sûret-i ilmiyesi mevcud olan bir şeyi kalbinde dilediği gibi parçalasın, tefrik etsin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every act of recollection is a kind of resurrection; the inner world of memory and will offers an accessible analogy for God's renewal of all existence.
rows.anchor: Her tezekkür bir ba‘stir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since all inner and outer creation lies under God's knowledge and will, the whole cosmos responds to His command Be even faster than human recollection.
rows.anchor: Allah’ın ba‘s u ihyâsı bizim bir tezekkürümüzden daha serî‘dir

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By fully returning to God and obeying the commands, Abraham witnessed cosmic revival inwardly, attained a living heart, and recognized that God creates life-givers as well as the living.
rows.anchor: Allah’ın yalnız hay değil muhyî dahi yarattığını görmüş, hem azîz, hem hakîm olduğunu anlamış

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophetic miracles and the mysteries of revival reflect God's power; denying their possibility assumes rival powers above creation, which is shirk and unbelief.
rows.anchor: Bunları kābil-i tasavvur görmemek kendinin karşısındaki hâricî âfâk gibi Allah’ın karşısında şürekâ-yı âfâk veya mâfevk farz etmekten neş’et eder

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only God brings people from darkness into light, through faith rather than compulsion; faith is reason's foundation, so one should submit to God's might and follow His wisdom.
rows.anchor: Bundan ancak Allah çıkarır, o da cebren değil iman ile çıkarır

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Resurrection and eternal happiness grow from deeds chosen in worldly life; the afterlife is the realm of effects, so people must turn to God, give, and strive before that day.
rows.anchor: insanların hayât-ı ûlâda mevzû‘-i din olan ef‘âl-i ihtiyâriyeleri de ber mûceb-i hikmet esbâb-ı ‘âdiye-i mütekaddimeden olacağı

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the resurrection day there will be no transaction, friendship, or intercession; those who do not voluntarily give and strive beforehand will wrong themselves and fall under tyrants.
rows.anchor: o ‘urve-i vüskāya yapışıp fî-sebîlillâh infak ve mücahede ile Allah’a rücû‘edenlerin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This account explains the wisdom behind the earlier command to spend and confirms God's ancient and enduring assurance that a good loan is multiplied.
rows.anchor: âyetindeki ilan ve va‘d-i ilâhînin ezelî ve ebedî te’mînât-ı yakīniyesini dahi muhtevî bulunduğundan
